transcript:
MEETING HEADER
Date: 2026-02-11
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes (recording)
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Jonas Reed (Redwood SE), Aisha Gomez (FinData SRE), Trevor Lane (FinData ML Infra), Rachel Kim (FinData Product)
Shared: deck: /redwood/scheduler-tuning-deck.pdf, bench spreadsheet: /redwood/benchmarks/finData-2-11.csv

SUMMARY:
Short deep dive on throughput governor, continuous batching, and token caps for FinData's customer-facing summarization endpoint. Goal: get 95th percentile latency under 180ms for 256-token responses while keeping cost within target (<=$0.0008/token) and exploring on-prem/VPC constraints.

TOPICS:
- Continuous batching behavior with peaky short requests
- Scheduler knobs: max_num_seqs, max_tokens_per_slot, priority windows
- Token limits and soft eviction vs hard blocking
- KV-cache eviction policy tuning and warmstart
- Quantization tradeoffs for small-medium models on dedicated pools
- On-prem/VPC networking impact on cold starts

TRANSCRIPT:
[00:00] Maya Patel: ok everyone hi, thanks for joining, we wanted to focus today on the throughput governor and some token limit strategies for the summarization API. Jonas will run through the runtime knobs and we'll map them to your traffic pattern, so Trevor maybe start with a 30 second on current SLOs?
[00:17] Trevor Lane: yeah sure thanks, so current SLO is p95 < 200ms, p99 < 350ms, most responses are roughly 200-300 tokens but the distribution has a long tail. We see bursts from the mobile clients around 9am PST and random spikes from batch syncs. Throughput peak about 3k rps for short requests but avg is 300 rps
[00:38] Jonas Reed: mm-hm, got it. When you say 200-300 tokens is that model tokens or post-processed chars? sometimes that changes the kv cache mileage
[00:47] Rachel Kim: model tokens, we're using an internal tokenizer. We trimmed some whitespace but otherwise raw model tokens.
[00:52] Jonas Reed: ok that helps. So the big levers are continuous batching window, max_num_seqs (max sequences allowed per slot), and token guards — we usually combine soft limits and a per-request token ceiling. I'll sketch a config we commonly use for peaky short requests.
[01:10] Jonas Reed: baseline: continuous batching window 20ms, max_num_seqs 64, max_tokens_per_slot 4096, token_guard soft 512 per request, with eviction score favoring age+prefix hitrate. In practice that lets short 32-64 token requests pack very well and keeps latency low.
[01:28] Aisha Gomez: can you explain soft limit vs hard? we saw some hard rejects in our logs when quota was reached
[01:33] Jonas Reed: yep — soft limit means the scheduler will deprioritize or push to next slot if it would exceed the soft threshold. Hard means immediate 429/rejection. Soft keeps throughput by sacrificing some latency for the offending requests. Hard is for strict quota enforcement but hurts p95.
[01:49] Maya Patel: and for FinData's SLAs I'd recommend soft by default and a fast fallback to a smaller quantized variant if latency gets out of range. Jonas, show the fallback path.
[01:58] Jonas Reed: sure. We can route to a quantized int8-variant in the same pool or to dedicated lower-cost nodes. Fallback policy is: if observed p95 > 180ms for 30s, route new requests to quantized model for 10% of traffic as a canary, then progressively increase.
[02:13] Trevor Lane: what's the cost delta there typically? int8 vs fp16?
[02:18] Jonas Reed: int8 usually gives 2-3x throughput uplift per GPU for autoregressive workloads, cost per token drops roughly 40-60% depending on batch packing and kv-hit. But quality regression is model-specific — we'll run evals on your prompt set.
[02:33] Aisha Gomez: you mentioned kv-hit, our hit rates are pretty low right now — like 8% — probably because prompts have per-user personalization. can we still benefit from kv?
[02:44] Jonas Reed: 8% is low but still helps for repeated prefixes. We can tune eviction so items with high reuse are kept. Also increase kv cache shard count and raise max_num_seqs so more prefixes remain resident. But that trades off with memory per sequence and reduces available packing.
[03:03] Rachel Kim: what about max_num_seqs — is that the same as max sequences per model instance? we had that set to 32 to reduce OOMs
[03:12] Jonas Reed: yes it's per-slot max. Increasing from 32 to 64 lets more short requests share KV and batched execution, but increases GPU memory for kv+activation. For your model on 80GB A100s we can probably go to 64 safely if we also enable per-seq activation compression (a quant-aware setting).
[03:30] Trevor Lane: activation compression? is that lossy?
[03:33] Jonas Reed: it's lossy at float-level but designed to be transparent in most completions — it's more like fp16-aware packing or block-quantization; we saw negligible quality drop on summarization tasks.
[03:45] Maya Patel: quick note — we've had customers call this compression 'activation quant' in some docs so you'll see naming variance
[03:51] Aisha Gomez: lol that's why docs are confusing. ok continuing, how does scheduler prioritize low-latency short requests vs large batch jobs we run nightly
[03:59] Jonas Reed: scheduler supports priority windows: you can reserve slots for short tail-latency priority buckets. Example: reserve 25% of slots for 'interactive' priority with max_num_seqs optimized for small seqs and smaller window times. Long batches go to the remaining capacity and can be throttled or scheduled off-peak.
[04:18] Trevor Lane: we do have nightly ETL that spikes tokens massively — can we configure preemption?
[04:22] Jonas Reed: yes preemption policy allowed: smallest-impact preemption first — i.e., drop or spill long-batch slots and move them to burst capacity or defer. There's also a 'graceful-evict' mode where long jobs are paused mid-generation and resumed.
[04:36] Rachel Kim: saving state mid-run seems tricky, is resume reliable?
[04:40] Jonas Reed: resume uses saved KV snapshots and sequence indexes; it's reliable for deterministic decoders, but for stochastic top-k samplers you may see slight variation. For your determinism-sensitive flows we can prefer top-p with fixed seeds.
[04:56] Maya Patel: ok let's talk about token ceilings — you mentioned a per-request ceiling and a slot ceiling
[05:01] Jonas Reed: right, per-request ceiling prevents runaway prompts. slot ceiling is the max aggregate tokens a slot will accept. For example slot ceiling 4096, per-request 1024 — if a request is 1200 tokens, it gets clipped or routed to a large-slot node.
[05:17] Aisha Gomez: can we implement dynamic clipping where long user prompts get summarized first client-side then sent to the model?
[05:23] Jonas Reed: yes that's a good pattern. Client-side pre-tokenization + light summarization reduces tokens while preserving context. We can provide a lightweight summarizer microservice running on the edge.
[05:33] Trevor Lane: you mentioned continuous batching window earlier — is 20ms always best?
[05:36] Jonas Reed: not always. 20ms is a good default for dense short request workloads; if your traffic is burstier with a lot of simultaneous arrivals, increasing to 40–60ms can improve packing with minimal p95 impact. Conversely, for ultra-low latency you drop to 5–10ms but packing suffers.
[05:53] Rachel Kim: what's the math behind choosing window vs max_num_seqs? do you have a formula?
[05:58] Jonas Reed: rough heuristic: expected batch size B = arrival_rate * window. Aim for B close to max_num_seqs but below it. So window = max_num_seqs / arrival_rate. But skew and jitter matter; run bench traces for accurate sizing.
[06:11] Trevor Lane: ok that makes sense. Let's hit some concrete benching - are you able to run an in-cluster run against our VPC tomorrow?
[06:17] Maya Patel: yes we typically do a 60–90 minute benchmark with sample traffic; needs a VPC peering and temporary keys. Jonas can coordinate the script.
[06:24] Jonas Reed: I'll share the script, it's the bench v2 with adjustable arrival curves. We'll need a representative prompt set and token histogram.
[06:31] Aisha Gomez: we'll export logs tonight, expect to send by EOD.
[06:34] Jonas Reed: great. A couple more knobs — token guard strategies: hard clip, soft clip, and progressive trimming. Progressive trimming reduces length iteratively until sequence fits, preserving early tokens.
[06:45] Rachel Kim: progressive trimming sounds neat for summaries — keep the intro but drop details.
[06:48] Jonas Reed: right we often preserve the most semantically dense prefixes based on a cheap scorer.
[06:53] Aisha Gomez: what about request prioritization by customer tier? we have platinum users
[06:57] Jonas Reed: we support token-credit debt and priority windows. Example: platinum gets tokens from priority pool, and non-platinum may be routed to spot/delayable pool.
[07:05] Trevor Lane: you mentioned VPC/on-prem differences — any cold-start differences we should know?
[07:10] Jonas Reed: networking overhead is slightly higher in on-prem because of private control-plane reachability and KMS calls. Cold-start can be 200–800ms higher when the model isn't warm; we mitigate with pre-warm slots and keep-alive pings.
[07:22] Maya Patel: we also have a small on-prem bundle that includes offline artifact cache to reduce KMS latency.
[07:27] Aisha Gomez: ok let's talk numbers — with window 30ms and max_num_seqs 64 what p95 should we see for 64-token responses?
[07:34] Jonas Reed: for your model and 80GB A100s I'd ballpark p95 ~ 120–160ms with KV hitrate 20%. Lower hitrate raises to 170–220ms. We'll need bench to validate.
[07:48] Trevor Lane: what about memory pressure — increasing max_num_seqs while also raising kv shards — what should we watch for?
[07:55] Jonas Reed: watch GPU reserved mem, OOM logs; we expose metrics: kv_mem_usage, activation_mem, free_mem, and per-slot seq count. We can set alerts on kv_mem_usage>75%.
[08:04] Rachel Kim: are there recommended safe defaults for our stack? summarize please
[08:08] Jonas Reed: sure: window 30ms, max_num_seqs 48–64, slot_ceiling 4096, per-request ceiling 1024, soft token guard enabled, kv_eviction policy LRU+reuse score, enable activation compression. That balances packing and memory.
[08:25] Maya Patel: Jonas can you describe a failure mode where these defaults would fail?
[08:29] Jonas Reed: very long prompt storms where many >1k token requests arrive simultaneously — packing will fail and you'll either see increased latency or hard 429s if you use hard guards. Another is very low kv hit (under 5%) combined with small windows — then batching doesn't help and you pay per-token cost.
[08:46] Aisha Gomez: how do we measure kv hit in your telemetry? is it per-route?
[08:50] Jonas Reed: yes it's per-route and per-model; we export kv_hits, kv_requests, kv_hit_rate, kv_evictions. We can add a tag for user_id if you need multi-tenant tracking.
[08:59] Trevor Lane: sounds good. On quantization — you said int8 might change behavior — any scheduler differences?
[09:05] Jonas Reed: quantized execution is faster per token but can have different memory patterns. For int8 we can increase max_num_seqs aggressively because activations shrink; but watch for kernel fallbacks — some ops may run slower on certain kernels so run a micro-bench.
[09:19] Rachel Kim: do you support mixed-mode pools (some GPUs int8, some fp16)?
[09:23] Jonas Reed: yes we call them variant pools. Smart routing will route to fastest compatible variant unless routing policy picks cheaper. Also automatic fallback if a variant runs out.
[09:33] Maya Patel: ok let's switch to a quick live config demo — Jonas are you able to show the dashboard? (screen share)
[09:37] Jonas Reed: sharing in a sec — sorry small lag — ok now you should see the scheduler dashboard with slot utilization graph, p95 latency, kv hit heatmap.
[09:50] Aisha Gomez: I can see it, the slot utilization looks spiky at 9am there — that's our mobile peak
[09:56] Jonas Reed: click the 'policy editor' and you'll see priority window rules and token guards. I'll edit a copy: change window to 40ms and max_num_seqs to 64 for the interactive route and save as 'fin-interactive-v1'.
[10:11] Jonas Reed: apply... it's queued to small rollout, not instant, but you can force canary to 5% of traffic for 10 minutes.
[10:20] Trevor Lane: let's canary it for 5% now
[10:22] Maya Patel: done, canary set. We'll watch p95 and kv hit.
[10:27] Jonas Reed: small note: canary to 5% may not show steady-state packing improvement but will show stability
[10:33] Aisha Gomez: ok watching metrics... p95 jumped to 190ms on the canary instances, any idea?
[10:38] Jonas Reed: may be due to cold kv shards; can you check kv_hit_rate on the canary nodes?
[10:44] Aisha Gomez: kv_hit rate 4% on canary versus 10% on baseline
[10:48] Jonas Reed: there we go — shard warming. We should allow a pre-warm phase or seed the cache with most common prefixes. Also the canary nodes may be on different hardware variant.
[10:56] Trevor Lane: we can try pre-warm, how long to warm to stable kv hit? maybe 10-20 minutes
[11:01] Jonas Reed: depends on traffic shape — 10-30 minutes typical for interactive prefixes. We can force-seed top N prefixes via a warmup job.
[11:08] Maya Patel: ok add warmup to action items. Anything else on the dashboard demo?
[11:13] Jonas Reed: just two more items: token-guard logs (helps debug why requests trimmed) and per-token cost estimator per route
[11:20] Rachel Kim: nice. about privacy — we need assurance on KMS and logs for VPC
[11:25] Maya Patel: we will send the private deployment security pack — includes KMS integration, audit logs, and SOC2 docs. I'll attach in follow-up.
[11:33] Aisha Gomez: thanks. for on-prem deployment, can we run the bench without sending data offsite?
[11:38] Jonas Reed: yes we support air-gapped bench agents; we'll provide a script and you can run locally and share metrics artifacts only.
[11:45] Trevor Lane: that would help our compliance team
[11:47] Maya Patel: noted, we'll add that option
[11:49] Jonas Reed: last technical note: autoscaling cooldown — short windows with aggressive autoscale can thrash. Use a 30s cooldown and scale by step (20% increments) rather than doubling.
[11:59] Maya Patel: good call. ok final recap?
[12:02] Maya Patel: Recap: Jonas to share bench script and policy template; FinData to provide token histogram and traces; we'll run bench in VPC with warmup; Maya to send security pack and pricing. Next meeting: bench review 2026-02-17 16:00 UTC.
[12:18] Aisha Gomez: confirmed
[12:20] Trevor Lane: thanks all
[12:22] Rachel Kim: thanks
[12:23] Maya Patel: thanks, meeting end
